where: Worked example 1 and Worked example 2 (and Section 2 formula v = πDN/60)
problem: The power step multiplies the whole friction force by the rim speed, v = πDN/60. In a rotating interface the rubbing speed falls linearly from that value at the rim to zero at the centre, so the true friction power is P = (2/3)πμpωR³, which is two-thirds of the number shown. Example 1 therefore gives 19.3 kW where the integrated result is about 12.9 kW; Example 2 gives 4.74 kW where the integrated result is about 3.16 kW. The arithmetic is right, but the model is never stated as an approximation, so a student who uses the correct integral in the exam will think the book is wrong.
fix: Add one line before step 4: 'The force is taken to act at the rim speed, an upper-bound estimate; a finer calculation integrates over the radius and gives 2/3 of this power.' Better still, add the formula P = (2/3)πμpωR³ with ω = 2πN/60 rad/s, R = radius in m, p = pressure in Pa, μ = coefficient of friction, and show both values.

problem: The trap says 'In friction welding one of the parts spins', but Section 2 and the bullet just above it describe linear friction welding, where nothing spins and one flat part oscillates. A student reading the trap list alone will contradict the earlier statement.
fix: Reword to 'In rotary friction welding one of the parts spins; in linear friction welding one flat part oscillates; in FSW a separate tool spins and both parts stay still.'
